title: WHY DID GOD FORBID A MAN FROM HAVING SEX WITH A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND LEVITICUS 18:17
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD FORBID A MAN FROM HAVING SEX WITH A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND LEVITICUS 18:17

One ancient command. Two generations of women. A devastating warning about lust, family betrayal, and the sacred boundaries God established to protect human dignity. But buried beneath this uncomfortable Scripture is a truth about sin, mercy, and redemption that every Christian needs to understand.
There are sins that destroy a marriage.
There are sins that tear a family apart.
And then there are sins so deeply entangled in betrayal that they can wound an entire generation before anyone realizes how much damage has been done.
Imagine a daughter sitting across the dinner table from her mother.
The man who once promised to love her mother is now looking at her in a way no father, stepfather, or trusted family member ever should.
At first, perhaps nobody notices.
A lingering glance. An inappropriate compliment. A conversation that should never have happened.
Then boundaries begin to disappear.
And suddenly, the very home that should have been a place of protection becomes a place of secrecy, confusion, and betrayal.
Now imagine opening your Bible and discovering that thousands of years ago, God spoke directly against a sexual relationship involving a woman and her daughter.
Not because He was embarrassed by sexuality.
Not because He hated pleasure.
And certainly not because He wanted to impose meaningless restrictions on human relationships.
But because the God who created the family also knows how profoundly sexual betrayal can destroy it.
And what makes this passage especially unsettling is that God did not describe the offense as merely inappropriate.
He used a Hebrew word that communicates something morally outrageous.
Something shameful.
Something that violates the boundaries of holiness.
But before we uncover that word, there is something important we must understand.

God's commandments are not always explanations of everything that could go wrong. Sometimes they are boundaries drawn by the One who already knows what human beings are capable of doing when desire becomes more important than love.
Listen carefully to the actual words of Scripture.
Leviticus 18:17 says in the King James Version:

“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness.”
Read that again.
A woman.
Her daughter.
Even her granddaughter.
God explicitly prohibited a man from taking these closely related women into sexual relationships.
And notice something that is easy to overlook.
The verse is not simply discussing adultery.
It is addressing sexual relationships that violate the boundaries of an interconnected family.
A man could not justify such conduct merely by claiming that everyone involved was willing or that he felt genuine affection.
Within Israel's covenant law, these relationships were forbidden because they crossed boundaries God had established.
But to understand why, we must go deeper than the English translation.
We must examine the Hebrew.
The original language of Leviticus 18:17 contains this expression:
שְׁאֵרָה הֵנָּה זִמָּה הִוא
Transliterated:
She'erah hennah, zimmah hi.
A careful translation is:
“They are her close relatives; it is depravity.”
The Hebrew word זִמָּה (zimmah) is particularly significant.
Depending on its context, the word can communicate wickedness, depravity, or a disgraceful scheme. In Leviticus 18:17, it describes the prohibited sexual relationship as a serious moral offense.

The Hebrew does not literally say that the daughter will become traumatized, that every family member will suffer a particular psychological consequence, or that the man has necessarily manipulated both women.
Those may be real dangers in particular situations, but they are not the literal translation of the verse.
The text itself makes a more specific declaration.
These women belong to the same close family relationship, and joining them to the same man sexually is prohibited.
That distinction matters.
Because if we want to honor God's Word, we must resist the temptation to make Scripture say more than it actually says.
The truth is already powerful enough.
Now consider the expression translated “uncover the nakedness.”
In Hebrew, the wording comes from the expression גִּלָּה עֶרְוָה (gillah 'ervah), meaning “to uncover nakedness.”
Within the sexual prohibitions of Leviticus 18, this is a conventional expression referring to prohibited sexual relations.
It is not merely a warning against accidentally seeing someone without clothing.
It concerns sexual intimacy and the boundaries governing it.
And the surrounding chapter makes those boundaries unmistakably important.
Leviticus 18 begins with God telling Israel not to imitate the practices of Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going.
The Lord then declares:
“Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD.” — Leviticus 18:5, KJV
God was forming a people who would live differently.
Their worship was to be different.
Their treatment of one another was to be different.
Their sexual conduct was to be different.
Their family relationships were to reflect boundaries that distinguished holiness from exploitation and disorder.
And this is where the passage begins to confront our modern world.
Because we live in a culture that often treats desire as its own justification.
“If it feels right, pursue it.”
“If both people agree, nobody should question it.”
“If it makes you happy, why should anyone interfere?”
But Scripture refuses to reduce sexual morality to the intensity of someone's feelings.
A desire can be powerful without being righteous.
An attraction can be sincere without being appropriate.
And a relationship can be emotionally complicated while still crossing a moral boundary.

That does not mean consent is unimportant. Consent is essential to distinguishing consensual conduct from coercion and abuse, but consent alone does not settle every question of biblical sexual ethics.
Leviticus 18:17 establishes a boundary that cannot simply be erased by mutual attraction.
Think about the implications.
A mother and daughter are not strangers competing for the attention of the same man.
They are family.
Their relationship exists independently of any romantic or sexual interest another person might have in them.
A mother should not have to experience her daughter as a sexual rival.
A daughter should not have to wonder whether the man involved with her mother is also pursuing her.
And a granddaughter should never be drawn into an intimate arrangement that disregards the generational boundaries of her family.
These observations help us appreciate the protective wisdom of the command, even though the verse itself does not provide a detailed account of every possible consequence.
Because a family is not merely a collection of individuals.
It is a network of trust.
And when sexual desire crosses certain family boundaries, the resulting betrayal can reach far beyond the people directly involved.
Sometimes the deepest wounds are not caused by strangers.
They are caused by people who were trusted to protect us.
Someone reading this may know exactly what that feels like.
Perhaps you grew up in a home where boundaries were never respected.
Perhaps an adult crossed a line and then convinced you to remain silent.
Perhaps someone used affection, religious authority, money, or emotional pressure to make you believe you had no right to object.
Perhaps your family protected its reputation while leaving you to carry the pain.
And perhaps you have spent years wondering whether God saw what happened.
Hear this carefully.
Being sexually exploited or abused is not the same as willingly committing the sin condemned in this passage.
If someone coerced you, manipulated you, threatened you, or violated you, the wrongdoing belongs to the person responsible for that abuse.
You do not have to accept blame for another person's violation of your dignity.
And you do not have to call evil good simply because the person responsible was a parent, relative, pastor, or someone respected by the community.
The God of Scripture does not command His people to conceal injustice.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
God's nearness to the brokenhearted does not mean every wound disappears immediately.
But it means suffering does not make someone invisible to Him.
And if this passage awakens painful memories, seeking safety, trustworthy support, and appropriate professional help is not a failure of faith.
It may be an important part of healing.
Yet there is another side of this command that we cannot ignore.
Because while some people have been wounded by the sins of others, some have knowingly crossed boundaries themselves.
Some have betrayed a spouse.
Some have pursued forbidden relationships.
Some have used another person's trust to satisfy selfish desires.
Some have justified what they knew was wrong because admitting the truth would require repentance.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about sin is how easily the human heart can become skilled at defending it.
We rename lust as love.
We rename betrayal as destiny.
We rename secrecy as privacy.
We rename rebellion as freedom.
And eventually, if we are not careful, we stop asking whether God approves and begin asking only whether we can get away with it.
But Scripture does not allow us to escape moral responsibility through clever language.
Jesus Himself confronted the condition of the human heart.
In Matthew 5:28, He said:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Jesus was not teaching that every involuntary attraction is equivalent to a completed act of adultery.
He was exposing the deliberate cultivation of lustful desire.
He was showing that sexual holiness is not merely about avoiding certain physical actions while privately feeding the desires that lead toward them.
God cares about the heart.
The intentions.
The choices.
The things we entertain when nobody else is watching.
And this is why Leviticus 18:17 should never become an opportunity for Christians to condemn a particular category of sinners while ignoring their own need for grace.
The man who has never committed this specific offense may still be guilty of lust.
The person who has never betrayed a family sexually may still have betrayed someone through dishonesty.
The person who can quote every verse about sexual purity may still be hiding pride, hypocrisy, or cruelty.
Romans 3:23 tells us:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
That word removes every pedestal.
Nobody stands before God justified by the fact that someone else's sin appears more shocking.
And yet this is where the story becomes far more extraordinary.
Because the Bible does not end with Leviticus.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
And when Jesus entered the world, He did not arrive among people who had perfectly preserved God's commandments.
He entered a world of broken families, damaged reputations, sexual sin, religious hypocrisy, and human suffering.
He encountered people whom society had already decided were beyond restoration.
And one of the most revealing encounters appears in John chapter 4.
Jesus met a Samaritan woman at a well.
She had experienced five marriages, and the man she was living with was not her husband.
We should be careful not to invent details Scripture does not give us. The passage does not explain why those marriages ended, nor does it tell us whether she was responsible for each separation.
What Scripture does reveal is that Jesus knew the truth about her life.
And He spoke to her anyway.
He did not pretend her circumstances were irrelevant.
But neither did He treat her as someone unworthy of hearing about the living water He could give.
Consider the contrast.
Human beings often use someone's history as a reason to dismiss them.
Jesus revealed His identity as the Messiah to a woman whose life contained complicated relationships and unresolved questions.
He knew her story.
And He offered her something greater than the life she had known.
Living water.
A new relationship with God.
The possibility of worshiping the Father in spirit and in truth.
That encounter does not erase the moral commands of Leviticus.
It reveals the heart of the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
Jesus did not come to convince humanity that sin was harmless.
He came because sin was serious enough to require His saving work.
And grace is not the declaration that wrongdoing never mattered.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness toward people who cannot save themselves.
Look at another encounter.
In John chapter 8, a woman accused of adultery was brought before Jesus.
The religious leaders wanted to use her case to trap Him.
They placed her shame in public view.
And Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of those who were eager to condemn her.
After her accusers departed, Jesus said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
It is important to acknowledge that John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and modern Bible editions commonly mark the passage as a later textual tradition.
Nevertheless, the account has long been influential in Christian teaching, and its central themes of mercy and repentance are consistent with teachings found elsewhere in the New Testament.
Notice the two truths held together in Jesus' words.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
He did not say, “Your actions do not matter.”
He did not say, “Continue as you were.”
But He also did not reduce the woman to her worst moment.
This is the tension that makes the Gospel so beautiful.
Jesus takes sin seriously enough to call us out of it, and loves sinners deeply enough to make redemption possible.
And that brings us back to the uncomfortable question at the beginning.
Why did God forbid sexual relations involving a woman and her daughter?
Because under the covenant law given to Israel, such relationships violated the boundaries God established among close family members.
Because the women were related to one another in a way the law treated as morally significant.
Because sexuality was not intended to be governed by appetite alone.
And because the holiness God required of His people extended into the most private areas of their lives.
The passage is not an isolated rule without context.
Leviticus 18 contains a series of prohibitions involving close relatives and other forbidden sexual practices.
Leviticus 20:14 returns to the issue of a man taking a woman and her mother, describing it as a grave offense under Israel's law and assigning a severe penalty within that ancient legal system.
Christians should not confuse those ancient civil penalties with permission to inflict violence today.
The New Testament calls believers to holiness, repentance, justice, and obedience to Christ, not private retaliation or the unauthorized enforcement of ancient Israel's penal laws.
And there is another important distinction.
Leviticus 18:17 is not primarily a discussion about a modern blended family, an ordinary stepfather caring appropriately for his stepdaughter, or a parent showing healthy affection to a child.
The command addresses prohibited sexual relations.
We must not stretch its meaning so carelessly that we create suspicion around innocent family relationships.
The boundary concerns sexual conduct.
And the moral seriousness of that boundary should lead us toward protection, faithfulness, and integrity.
But perhaps you are asking a more personal question.
What if I have already crossed a boundary?
What if I have done something I cannot undo?
What if the person I betrayed will never trust me again?
What if I have confessed to God but still cannot forgive myself?
This is where Christianity offers something far more substantial than empty reassurance.
It offers the Gospel.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance.
It refers to a change of mind or turning, and in biblical teaching it involves a genuine reorientation toward God that bears fruit in changed conduct.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after being exposed.
It is not crying because consequences have arrived.
It is not asking God to remove the embarrassment while secretly planning to continue the behavior.
Real repentance agrees with God's judgment about sin.
It stops defending what is wrong.
It turns toward Christ.
And where another person has been harmed, repentance includes taking responsibility rather than demanding immediate forgiveness or reconciliation.
Sometimes repentance means confessing a hidden wrong.
Sometimes it means ending an inappropriate relationship.
Sometimes it means accepting boundaries that protect the people you have harmed.
Sometimes it means submitting to legal accountability.
Sometimes it means understanding that forgiveness from God does not automatically restore access to someone else's life.
Grace is not permission to escape the consequences of our choices.
But neither is repentance a hopeless attempt to earn what only Jesus can give.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Read that promise carefully.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Not because sin was imaginary.
Not because the damage was insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior whose sacrifice provides the foundation for forgiveness.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The resurrection is Christianity's declaration that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And this is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not simply a memorable phrase.
It is a testimony to what the Gospel proclaims.
From Scandal to Grace. Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
But we must understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending the wrong never happened.
He does not erase the dignity of victims to protect the reputation of offenders.
He does not demand that wounded people trust those who remain dangerous.
He does not call unrepentant abuse a beautiful redemption story.
He transforms people through truth, repentance, mercy, and new life.
A person who once lived in secrecy can learn to walk in the light.
A person who once pursued selfish pleasure can learn sacrificial love.
A person who once betrayed trust can begin taking responsibility for the harm they caused.
A person who has suffered because of another's wrongdoing can discover that their identity is not defined by what was done to them.
And sometimes restoration looks different from what we imagined.
A marriage may not be repaired.
A relationship may never resume.
A family may require lasting boundaries.
But the absence of a particular reconciliation does not mean God has abandoned the work of redemption.
His grace is not limited to giving us back the exact life we had before.
Sometimes His grace leads us into a different life altogether.
One built on truth.
One shaped by humility.
One no longer controlled by secrecy.
And if you are reading this while carrying guilt, there is something you need to hear.
You cannot change yesterday.
You cannot return to the moment before the wrong decision.
You cannot force someone to trust you again.
But you can stop running from the truth today.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can seek help.
You can make the changes that obedience requires.
And you can come to Jesus Christ without pretending that you have anything to boast about.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people never fall.
It is the announcement that salvation comes through Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
The apostle Paul wrote to believers in Corinth after naming serious patterns of sinful conduct, including sexual immorality.
Then he declared:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Such were some of you.
Four words that carry an astonishing message.
Your past may explain where you have been.
But through Christ, it does not have to dictate who you become.
This does not mean transformation is always instant or that every struggle disappears.
It means that belonging to Jesus brings a new identity and calls us into a new way of life.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not by hiding the truth.
But through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why this difficult passage deserves our attention today.
Because Leviticus 18:17 is not merely about something ancient Israelites were forbidden to do.
It confronts the temptation to place our desires above the well-being of others.
It reminds us that family relationships are not disposable.
It challenges the idea that secrecy can make wrongdoing acceptable.
And it calls us to recognize that God's holiness reaches into the places we are most tempted to keep hidden.
If you are a husband, love your wife faithfully.
If you are a father or stepfather, protect the dignity and boundaries of every child entrusted to your care.
If you are a mother, remember that your daughter is not your competitor.
If you are a young person being pressured into secrecy by someone older or more powerful, understand that you have the right to seek safety and tell someone trustworthy.
If you are a Christian leader, never use Scripture, spiritual authority, or religious language to excuse exploitation.
And if you are someone who has committed sexual wrongdoing, do not use the language of grace to avoid repentance.
The same Savior who welcomes sinners also calls them to follow Him.
He calls us away from darkness.
Away from deception.
Away from the kind of desire that treats people as objects.
And toward a love that reflects His own.
A love that is truthful.
A love that protects.
A love that does not exploit.
A love that seeks another person's good even when obedience requires sacrifice.
Maybe this article has brought something uncomfortable to the surface.
A memory.
A conviction.
A hidden compromise.
A wound you have never spoken about.
Or perhaps it has simply reminded you that God's commandments contain wisdom we should not dismiss merely because our culture finds them inconvenient.
Whatever brought you here, do not leave with information alone.
Bring what you have heard before the Lord.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need protection, seek it.
If you need healing, allow yourself to pursue it.
If you need to forgive, ask God for wisdom about what forgiveness means without surrendering healthy boundaries.
And if you have been treating your relationship with Jesus as something you can postpone indefinitely, remember that tomorrow is not promised.
Come to Him today.
Not because an article frightened you.
Not because a religious page pressured you.
But because Christ is worthy of your trust, your obedience, and your life.
And if you do not know how to begin, you can pray sincerely:

“Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know the things I have confessed and the things I have tried to hide. You know where I have sinned, and You know where I have been wounded. I do not want to keep running from Your truth. Forgive my sins, teach me genuine repentance, and help me walk in holiness. Give me courage to take responsibility where I have done wrong and wisdom to seek safety where I have been harmed. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Teach me to trust You, follow You, and live in the freedom of Your grace. Amen.”
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not to pressure you into publicly revealing something private.
But because sometimes a simple, honest response becomes the beginning of a meaningful conversation.
What spoke to your heart most deeply: God's boundaries, the seriousness of sin, or the possibility of redemption through Jesus Christ?
If you are still struggling but refuse to abandon your faith, you can comment, “I'm still fighting.”
If you need encouragement and prayer, comment, “Pray for me.”
If you have experienced God's mercy and want to testify without sharing private details, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if this passage has changed how you understand God's holiness, share what you learned. Your reflection may help another person read Scripture more carefully.
Sometimes the most meaningful testimony is simply acknowledging that you need His grace.
And please do not allow this message to end with you.
Not to expose or humiliate anyone.
Not to win an argument.
But because someone among your family, friends, and followers may be struggling with questions about sexuality, biblical holiness, guilt, or forgiveness.
Someone may have misunderstood this passage for years.
Someone may be carrying shame that only grows heavier in silence.
Someone may desperately need to hear that Jesus Christ offers forgiveness to the repentant and compassion to the wounded.
Because spiritual growth should never be reduced to a passing emotional moment.
It requires returning to Scripture.
Learning.
Praying.
Repenting.
Obeying.
And walking with Jesus when nobody is applauding.
We want biblical nourishment and opportunities for spiritual growth to remain accessible to people who may not have the means to purchase books or study materials.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you during difficult seasons, or pointed you toward Christ, I want to extend a personal invitation.

It is voluntary financial support that can help sustain the work of creating biblical articles, sharing Gospel-centered teaching, maintaining free discipleship resources, and expanding the ministry's reach.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not a promise that financial support will purchase God's favor.
But a willing partnership in work you believe is helping people encounter biblical truth.
These products can be reminders of faith and practical ways to share the Gospel Warrior message, but they are never substitutes for Scripture, prayer, or a personal relationship with Jesus Christ.
Invite others to read it.
Pray for those who are struggling.
And above all, live the truth you have learned.
Because our greatest purpose is not simply to build an audience.
It is to point people to Jesus Christ.
The Savior who does not excuse sin.
The Savior who does not abandon the brokenhearted.
The Savior who calls us to repentance and offers forgiveness through His grace.
The Savior who makes new life possible.
Leviticus 18:17 reminds us that God draws boundaries around what is sacred.
The Gospel reminds us that when human beings have crossed those boundaries, Jesus Christ remains the only Savior who can redeem sinners.
And when those boundaries have been violated against us, His compassion reminds us that our dignity is not destroyed by another person's wrongdoing.
That is why we must preach both truth and grace.
Because truth without compassion can become cruelty.
And grace without repentance can become an excuse to remain unchanged.
But in Jesus Christ, we encounter the holy God who tells the truth about sin and the merciful Savior who opens the way to redemption.
Your darkest chapter may be part of your history, but it does not have to be the final word over your life in Christ.
